subject: physics_2
question_text: What is 'Doppler effect'? Give illustrative examples.

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this paper: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers, so neither check was run. Physics hand-checked: for a source moving toward a stationary observer n′ = n·V/(V − Vₛ) > n, and moving away n′ = n·V/(V + Vₛ) < n — the same formulas the book derives in the Long Answer section. The book's example spellings ('peroson') are corrected.

recall_prompt: Say the definition of the Doppler effect, then the two train examples with the apparent-frequency formula for each.

steps.label: The definition
steps.mark_note: Apparent change due to relative motion
lines: The apparent change in the frequency of
sound heard by an observer, due to
relative motion between the source and
the observer, is called the Doppler
steps.margin_note: First mark. Apparent change and relative motion are the two phrases the examiner checks.
steps.why: The source's own frequency never changes — only what the observer hears. Naming the cause as RELATIVE motion covers both cases: a moving source and a moving observer.
common_mistakes: Dropping the word apparent — the emitted frequency is constant.
Writing motion of the source only — the effect also appears when the observer moves.

recall.must_convey: That the Doppler effect is the apparent change in heard frequency caused by relative motion between source and observer.
accept: relative motion between source and observer
the heard frequency changes, not the emitted one

steps.memory_tip: Apparent + relative: the frequency only seems to change, and either party may be the one moving.

steps.label: Example — approaching train
lines: approaches a station, a person standing
on the platform hears the frequency of
the whistle increase, because the train
is in relative motion toward the
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The first illustration: source approaching, frequency appears higher.
steps.why: As the source closes in, each successive sound crest is emitted from a nearer point, so the crests reach the ear more closely spaced — more per second, a higher heard frequency.
common_mistakes: Saying the whistle becomes louder — the effect changes the frequency (pitch), not the loudness.

recall.must_convey: That the whistle of an approaching train appears higher in frequency to a person on the platform.
accept: the crests arrive more closely spaced

steps.memory_tip: Closing in packs the crests together — more arrive each second.

steps.label: Apparent frequency, approaching
lines: For a source moving toward a stationary
observer with velocity Vₛ (V = speed of
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Minus sign in the denominator for approach — the fraction exceeds 1.
steps.why: The denominator V − Vₛ is smaller than V, so the fraction is greater than 1 and n′ comes out above n — the formula agrees with the example it describes, which is the quickest sanity check in the exam.
common_mistakes: Using the plus sign for approach — V + Vₛ gives n′ < n, the receding case.
Putting Vₛ in the numerator — the source's motion changes the wavelength, which sits in the denominator.

recall.must_convey: That for an approaching source n′ = nV/(V − Vₛ), which is greater than n.
accept: n prime is n V by V minus V s
minus in the denominator for approach
n prime is greater than n
reject: V plus V s in the denominator

steps.memory_tip: Approach shrinks the denominator, so the frequency grows — the sign always matches the story.

lines.text: Approaching: n′ > n · Receding: n′ < n

steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. The mirror case: plus sign, fraction below 1, frequency lower.
steps.why: Moving away stretches the spacing between crests, so fewer reach the ear each second; the plus sign in the denominator makes the fraction less than 1, matching the lower heard frequency.
common_mistakes: Writing the same formula for both cases — the two differ only in the sign of Vₛ, and the sign IS the physics.

recall.must_convey: That for a receding source the heard frequency falls, n′ = nV/(V + Vₛ) < n.
accept: n prime is n V by V plus V s
plus in the denominator for receding

steps.memory_tip: Away stretches the crest spacing — plus in the denominator, lower pitch.

insider_note: The two formulas differ only in one sign, and that sign is where the marks move — check each against its own story: approach must give n′ > n.
